Case Study

Student Loan Education

A self-paced course that helps college students locate, understand, and plan for their federal student loans before they graduate. A class assignment and passion project, not live at Asbury Financial Aid.

Watch the Project Overview Back to Portfolio
Context

Final project for ID 212 at Asbury University, designed for the Discovery (D2L) LMS

Audience

Full-time undergraduates, ages 18 to 22

My Role

Sole Multimedia Instructional Designer and developer

Tools

Adobe Express, Adobe Firefly (Katie's learner portrait), ElevenLabs, Articulate 360, Canva, Boords, Discovery (D2L), NotebookLM and ChatGPT (organizing research and drafting outlines)

Framework

Backward design, action mapping, Learning Experience Canvas

Status

Class assignment. Full three-module course designed, Module 1 built. Not live at Asbury Financial Aid.

The Problem

Graduates hit by loan numbers they never learned to read

I watched my older sister and my best friend graduate and get hit by their final loan amounts and monthly interest. I found it wasn't isolated. My friends, when I asked them, couldn't even remember their principal amounts, much less the compounded interest rates. I saw the same confusion across my family and their friends.

As a junior I was looking for a resource like this and couldn't find one, so this became a passion project. My Five Whys analysis traced the root cause to student loan literacy not being part of required curriculum, with the assumption that students get guidance from family, friends, or the internet.

The Solution

A short, self-paced course built around "Katie"

A short, asynchronous, mobile-friendly course on Discovery, built around a learner persona named Katie. It has three one-hour modules, each following the same pattern: video, activity, quiz, personal application, survey, and resources.

Quizzes allow unlimited attempts and are open book, and the course is graded pass/fail on mastery, so learners can take whatever time they need to feel ready to move on.

Module 1: Locating and Identifying Loan Types (built). Module 2: Calculating Interest. Module 3: Repayment and Strategy.

The Process

How I built it

1

Spotting the Need

I spotted the need through personal experience, observing family and friends, and informal conversations, including three one-on-one interviews with friends.

2

Root Cause Analysis

I used Five Whys to trace the problem back to its root cause: student loan literacy is not part of the required curriculum.

3

Building the Learner Persona

I built the persona of Katie from my learner analysis: a full- or part-time college student, ages 18 to 22, who is motivated to understand her loans and pay them off efficiently, and who does not want to be caught off guard by interest rates or hidden fees.

4

Choosing a Framework

I chose backward design and mapped the course with the Learning Experience Canvas and action mapping.

5

Objectives and Rubric

I wrote three learning objectives and a mastery-based, pass/fail rubric.

6

Storyboarding

I storyboarded the lecture in Boords, writing the voice-over and scene directions for each frame.

My storyboard sketches for the Student Loan module, from the welcome screen to course completion.

7

Producing the Lecture

I produced a narrated, animated lecture using motion design, video editing, and audio editing in Adobe Express. I animated the on-screen text, timed scenes and transitions to the narration, and edited the ElevenLabs-generated voice and music myself.

The storyboard in Boords, then the animated lecture timeline in Adobe Express.

8

Designing the Handouts

I designed the Canva "At a Glance" handout and the "Snapshot" worksheet, where learners log in to their own federal loan portal and record their loan types, principal, and total amount.

9

Building the Scenario Activity

I built a scenario activity in Articulate 360 where learners guide Katie through a simulated federal loan portal.

10

Assembling the Module in Discovery

I assembled the module in Discovery (D2L) with the lecture, activity, quiz, survey, and resources.

Results and Takeaways

What happened when I presented it

Professor Feedback

"Aleia, this is an excellent course! Your use of AI is exactly what you should do in the real world of work as an ID. All of your components are excellent. ... I think you should reach out to Asbury financial aid and let them see what you created. They might have suggestions and then actually use it in the future."

Course ProfessorAsbury University

Personal Takeaways

I learned to stop complaining about an issue and actually do something about it. That is easier said than done. Moving from frustration into action without clear guidelines made me pause, reflect, and critically evaluate what would be most helpful to me and my friends before I proposed a solution.
